opus-5.5.text:
I think this is one of the most important questions for anyone building in this space right now. Large model companies can copy any single product feature very quickly, and they have more compute, more talent, and more distribution. So if your innovation is just one clever feature or one good prompt wrapped in a nice interface, it will be copied, and probably within a few months.

But I don't think that means startups have no chance. You have to think about what is actually hard to copy. Model companies are optimizing for very general capabilities. They want to serve hundreds of millions of users with one interface, so they naturally go after the biggest, most general use cases. A startup can go deep into a specific context: a specific workflow, a specific group of users, specific data and feedback loops that the big company doesn't have and doesn't care enough about to build.

Another thing I've been thinking about is that in the AI era, a lot of the value is shifting from the model to the environment and the context. Who owns the user's context, their memory, their tools, their workflow? If a startup builds a product where the context accumulates over time and becomes more useful the more you use it, that's much harder to copy than a feature. The big company can copy your UI, but it can't copy your users' history or the trust you've built in a particular vertical.

Speed and taste also matter. Big companies have their own priorities, organizational overhead, and many things competing for attention. A small team with very good taste about what the product should feel like can iterate much faster and find the right form for a new capability before anyone else.

So my view is: don't compete on things the model company will naturally get for free as models improve. If your product gets worse or becomes irrelevant when the next model comes out, that's a dangerous position. You want to build something that gets better when the models get better. That's probably the clearest test for whether a startup's innovation can survive being copied.

r001.rationale: It says large model companies can quickly copy a startup’s product feature and UI.

r002.rationale: It describes startups finding specific workflows and contexts, but does not say startups gain an opportunity when model developers fail to apply their own models effectively.

r003.rationale: It says products should improve as models improve, but does not state that stronger model capabilities let large companies make a startup’s interaction design work well.

fable-5.1.text:
I think this is actually one of the most interesting structural questions right now, and I'd push back a little on how it's usually framed. People talk about it as if it's a kind of theft, like the big labs are watching what the startups build and just absorbing it. But I'd say it's closer to a natural division of labor, and the question for a startup isn't "how do I avoid being copied," it's "what am I doing that's actually hard to copy."

Here's how I'd break it down. A large model company has a very specific set of advantages: they have the model, they have the compute, they have distribution, and crucially, they can see what's working across the entire ecosystem. If some wrapper product gets traction, they notice. So anything that is essentially a thin layer on top of the model, a clever prompt, a nice UI for a single use case, that layer is very cheap for them to replicate. And honestly, in many cases it's cheaper for them, because they can bake it into the model itself rather than building it on the outside. We saw this with a lot of early ChatGPT-era products. The "innovation" was really just being first to notice something the model could already do.

But I don't think that means startups are doomed. It means the frontier of defensibility has moved. If I look at what the big labs are structurally bad at, it's a few things. One is deep vertical context, really understanding a specific domain, the workflows, the data, the regulatory constraints, the way a lawyer or a biologist or a logistics manager actually spends their day. The labs are horizontal by nature. They want one model that does everything, and that pulls them away from going deep. The second is proprietary data loops, where the product generates signal that makes the product better and that signal isn't available to anyone else. And the third is, frankly, taste and speed on the long tail. There are thousands of niches where the labs will never prioritize you.

The other thing I'd say, and this comes from my own experience working on agents, is that a lot of what looks like "product innovation" is actually research that hasn't finished yet. When something like ReAct or tool use shows up first in a paper or a scrappy demo, and then shows up later inside a frontier model, people say "the lab copied it." But I'd say that's the idea completing its natural lifecycle. The ideas that are truly about how to use the model better will get absorbed into the model. That's almost definitional. So if your startup's moat is a better way of using the model, you should expect it to be absorbed, and you should plan your business around being one step ahead of that, or around something else entirely.

So my view is: don't compete on the layer that is closest to the model, because that layer is the labs' home turf and it's shrinking toward zero. Compete on the layers that touch the real world, specific users, specific data, specific trust relationships. The labs want to be the electricity. Fine, let them. The question is what you build that runs on electricity that they can't easily build themselves.

And one more thing, there's also a symbiotic side people underweight. Startups are, in a sense, the lab's distributed experimentation layer. They explore the space of what the model can do far faster than any one company could internally. The labs benefit enormously from that, and the smart ones know it. So the relationship isn't purely predatory. It's more like an ecosystem where the center keeps expanding and the periphery has to keep moving outward. If you're a startup and you understand that dynamic, you can actually use it rather than be a victim of it.

r001.rationale: The response says large labs notice successful startup products and may replicate or absorb their innovations into the model.

r002.rationale: It does not state that model developers fail to use their own models effectively or that this failure creates an opportunity for startups.

r003.rationale: It says model-use ideas can be absorbed into frontier models, but does not say stronger model capabilities let large companies make startup interaction designs work well.

astra-6.text:
我觉得不能简单地把这个关系理解成“大公司抄创业公司”。一个产品创新如果被验证有效，其他公司会跟进，这很正常。真正需要问的是：这个创新只是一个容易复制的功能，还是背后有一套持续发现用户需求、解决问题的能力？

如果创业公司的优势只是给模型加一个界面，或者把某个能力包装成一个功能，那模型公司下一次更新确实可能把它覆盖掉。但反过来，大模型公司也不可能把所有场景都做深。创业公司有机会更贴近具体用户，把产品嵌入他们的工作流程。这里面很多细节，并不是模型能力更强就能自动解决的。

所以我觉得，关键不是保证别人永远不做你做的东西，而是在别人开始跟进的时候，你是不是已经对问题有了更深的理解，能继续往前走。当然，如果你的产品每往前走一步，都恰好是模型公司下一步会顺手做掉的事情，那就需要认真思考自己的定位了。

r001.rationale: The response says that when an innovation proves effective, other companies follow, and notes that a model company may later absorb a startup’s feature.

r002.rationale: It says large model companies cannot deeply serve every scenario, creating room for startups, but does not say that developers fail to apply their own models effectively.

r003.rationale: The response says stronger model capability does not automatically solve workflow details; it does not present stronger model capability as a way to make startup interaction design work well.

sol-6.1.text:
I think there’s a real tension here. A startup can discover a useful interaction or a new way to package a model, and a large model company can incorporate that into its own product. If the startup’s entire advantage is that one feature, then its position is quite fragile.

But I wouldn’t reduce the relationship to copying. Both sides are exploring what these models make possible, so some convergence is natural. The more useful question for a startup is: what keeps getting stronger as you build? Is it your understanding of a particular workflow, your relationship with users, or your ability to deliver a complete solution? Those advantages are harder to reproduce than an interface.

And better models can help startups, too. A capability that competes with one startup might enable many others. So you have to keep asking: when the next model gets better, does our product become more valuable, or does the need for it disappear? That’s a pretty important distinction.

r001.rationale: It says a startup can discover a useful interaction or packaging approach and a large model company can incorporate it into its product.

r002.rationale: It does not say that a model developer’s failure to use its own models effectively creates an opening for startups.

r003.rationale: It says better models can help startups, but does not identify stronger model capabilities as a way for large companies to make a startup’s interaction design work well.
